```{r}
library(adempR)
```

A simulation estimates each performance measure from a finite number of
replications, so each reported value has Monte Carlo error. adempR reports
a Monte Carlo standard error (MCSE) for every built in measure, using the
formulas below. Write $\hat\theta_i$ for the estimate in replication $i$,
$\theta$ for the truth, $\widehat{SE}_i$ for the model based standard
error, and $n$ for the number of eligible replications.

```{r}
sim_measure_info()[c("measure", "eligibility", "direction")]
```

## Measures based on means

| Measure | Value | MCSE |
|---|---|---|
| bias | $\bar{\hat\theta} - \theta$ | $s_{\hat\theta} / \sqrt n$ |
| relbias | $(\bar{\hat\theta} - \theta) / \theta$ | $s_{\hat\theta} / (\lvert\theta\rvert \sqrt n)$ |
| mae | $\overline{\lvert\hat\theta - \theta\rvert}$ | $s_{\lvert\hat\theta-\theta\rvert}/\sqrt n$ |
| mse | $\overline{(\hat\theta - \theta)^2}$ | $s_{(\hat\theta-\theta)^2}/\sqrt n$ |
| mean_se | $\overline{\widehat{SE}}$ | $s_{\widehat{SE}}/\sqrt n$ |
| width | $\overline{U_i - L_i}$ | $s_{U-L}/\sqrt n$ |

Relative bias is a ratio, not a percentage. It is undefined (status
`"undefined"`) when the truth is 0. When the truth varies between data sets
it is the ratio of sums $\sum(\hat\theta_i - \theta_i) / \sum\theta_i$
with a delta method MCSE.

## Nonlinear measures

**RMSE** is $\sqrt{\text{MSE}}$ with delta method MCSE
$\text{MCSE(MSE)} / (2\,\text{RMSE})$.

**Empirical SE** is $s_{\hat\theta}$. Its MCSE uses the variance of the
sample variance without assuming normality,

$$\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(s^2) = \frac{1}{n}\left(m_4 - s^4 \frac{n-3}{n-1}\right),\qquad \text{MCSE}(s) = \frac{\sqrt{\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(s^2)}}{2 s},$$

where $m_4$ is the fourth central sample moment. For normal estimates this
reduces to the familiar $s / \sqrt{2(n-1)}$. If the estimate of
$\operatorname{Var}(s^2)$ is not positive, the normal theory value is
used.

**RMVAR**, the root mean of the model variances
$\sqrt{\overline{\widehat{SE}^2}}$, is the right comparator for the
empirical SE, because averaging variances, not standard errors, is what
makes the two comparable. Its MCSE is the delta method
$s_{\widehat{SE}^2}/(2\sqrt n\,\text{RMVAR})$.

**Relative error in model SE** is
$100\,(\text{RMVAR} / \text{EmpSE} - 1)$. Morris, White and Crowther
(2019, Table 6) give the MCSE

$$100\,\frac{\text{RMVAR}}{\text{EmpSE}}\sqrt{\frac{\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\widehat{SE}^2)}{4 n\,\text{RMVAR}^4} + \frac{1}{2(n-1)}},$$

which assumes approximately normal estimates and ignores the covariance
between the reported variances and the empirical variance. adempR reports
a jackknife MCSE over replications, which includes that covariance, and
gives the Table 6 value in the note. The test suite checks the point value
and the Table 6 value against `rsimsum`.

## Proportions

Coverage, the two one-sided noncoverages,
rejection and the usable proportion are proportions $\hat p = k / n$. Their
MCSE is $\sqrt{\hat p (1 - \hat p) / n}$, and the reported interval is the
exact Clopper-Pearson interval. When $\hat p$ is 0 or 1 the plug in MCSE is
0, which would claim certainty; the summary therefore marks such cells
with status `"boundary"` and the exact interval keeps a nonzero width.

Bias-eliminated coverage checks whether each interval contains its truth
shifted by the mean error, $\theta_r + \overline{(\hat\theta - \theta)}$;
for a constant truth that is $\bar{\hat\theta}$. It separates poor
coverage due to bias from poor coverage due to wrong width. The same
replications estimate the shift, so the indicators are dependent and the
binomial interval does not apply: its MCSE comes from a delete-a-group
jackknife that re-estimates the shift, with a normal interval.

## Eligibility and status

Each measure has its own denominator: bias needs a usable estimate and a
truth; mean SE needs a valid SE; coverage needs a valid interval; rejection
needs a valid test; the usable proportion and `usable_coverage` use all
generated data sets. The summary reports `n_eligible` for each cell,
`n_units`, the number of independent units behind it (replications, or
antithetic pairs; see below), and a `status`:

* `ok`
* `no_eligible`: no replication qualified
* `insufficient`: one replication, so no MCSE
* `degenerate`: all values equal, so a ratio or SE is undefined
* `infinite`: an infinite estimate entered the mean
* `boundary`: a proportion of 0 or 1, or with antithetic pairs a
  proportion whose pair means are all equal
* `overflow`: the empirical SE or its MCSE is not representable in double
  precision (the moments are computed on a common scale, so this happens
  only for spreads near the largest double)
* `unstable`: a ratio whose denominator is small relative to its Monte
  Carlo error (relative bias near a zero truth)
* `undefined`: for example relative bias with zero truth
* `unavailable`: the truth is unknown
* `incomplete`: for `usable` and `usable_coverage`, some generated data
  sets have not been analyzed yet (for example after an interrupted run);
  the note gives the bounds over all generated data sets
* `mcse_unavailable`: no known MCSE, for a custom measure without one or
  when the jackknife is undefined (for the SE ratio, leaving one
  replication out can leave estimates that are all equal)

## Antithetic pairs

With `sim_generator(antithetic = TRUE)` the two replications of a pair
are dependent, so the pair is the unit. For a measure that is a mean of
one contribution per replication the MCSE is computed in closed form from
the pair sums (the delete-one-pair jackknife, without refitting); for
other measures the delete-one-pair jackknife refits the measure. A
proportion whose pair means are all equal would get an MCSE of 0; its
interval is then the exact interval from the number of pairs with both
members at 1 and with at least one member above 0, out of `n_units`
pairs, and the status is `boundary`.

## Monte Carlo truth

When the truth is itself estimated, its error does not shrink with more
replications. The summary adds `truth_se`, `mcse_total` (for bias,
$\sqrt{\text{MCSE}^2 + SE_\text{truth}^2}$), and a sensitivity range for
measures that compare each estimate with the truth: the smallest and
largest value while the truth moves over $\pm 2\,SE_\text{truth}$
(the whole range, not only its two ends). A numerical truth with an error
bound gets the same range over plus and minus the bound. The point value
and its MCSE are conditional on the approximate truth.

## Custom measures

`sim_measure()` defines a measure by a per replication contribution and,
optionally, an aggregate. If no aggregate is given, the value is the mean
of the contributions and the MCSE is their standard deviation over
$\sqrt n$. If an aggregate is given (for example a median), no MCSE is
claimed unless the aggregate returns one.

```{r}
median_abs_error <- sim_measure("medae",
  contribution = function(rows) abs(rows$estimate - rows$truth),
  aggregate = function(x) list(value = median(x)),
  requires = "truth", direction = "lower")
sim_measures("bias", "coverage", median_abs_error)
```

## Streaming summaries

For very large runs, `sim_accumulator()` keeps means, variances and a
covariance that can be merged exactly across batches (the pairwise update
of Chan, Golub and LeVeque), so summaries can be built without holding all
replications in memory.

```{r}
x <- rnorm(1000)
acc <- sim_merge(sim_accumulate(sim_accumulator(), x[1:300]),
                 sim_accumulate(sim_accumulator(), x[301:1000]))
unlist(sim_accumulated(acc))
c(mean(x), var(x))
```
